title: Faith at the workplace
hookLine: keeping the turban and kara at work, and explaining kindly
tomorrow: Simran's pay is an hour short. does she bring it up?

lines: WHY IS YOUR BRACELET NOT PRETTY?
cards: Steel on steel makes a bright little clink. Every time Simran sets a bag on the scale pan, her kara taps the metal.
On Saturday a little boy holding his dad's hand watches it happen three times, then asks, very seriously: why is your bracelet not pretty? His dad turns pink and starts to apologize. Simran laughs.
She's heard her own dad answer harder questions than this.

teach.h: THE KARA: PLAIN STEEL, NOT JEWELRY.
teach.b: The kara is one of the five Ks: a plain band of steel or iron worn on the wrist. It isn't jewelry, so it isn't meant to be pretty.
A Sikh keeps it on at work like anywhere else, the way Simran's dad, Harjit, keeps his turban, his dastar, on at every truck stop between here and the next state.

He's been asked about it at counters and gas pumps for years, and his rule is simple: answer the question that was actually asked, kindly, in one breath, and let them ask the next one if they want to.
So Simran tries it on a very small person. It's a reminder, she says. It goes all the way around, no start and no end.

teach.h: NO START, NO END; HANDS FOR GOOD.
teach.b: And when I see it on my hand, I remember to use my hands for good things. The boy nods and asks if he can tap it. He taps it.
Clink. A common Sikh explanation of the kara runs just like that: a circle with no end, on the hand that works. The Granth doesn't describe the kara; it belongs to the rehat, the code of conduct.
But its spirit is close to a line of Guru Nanak's on ang 62, in paraphrase: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living.
Faith at work isn't a speech. It's a plain thing, kept on, and an answer short enough for a kid.

how: Sikhs keep their articles of faith, such as the kara and the turban, at work as everywhere else, and may explain them briefly when coworkers or customers ask.

games.q: what does “faith at the workplace” mean?
o: keeping religion completely out of sight on the job
keeping and kindly explaining your faith at work
preaching your religion to coworkers on breaks

games.q: faith on the job — tap the pairs.
p: a plain steel band, no start or end

games.q: a new coworker asks your Sikh friend, a bit too loudly, whether his turban is 'for a costume party'. going by today, what's the move?
o: answer what was asked, kindly, in one breath, and let them ask more.
give a long talk on Sikh history so they never ask again.
laugh it off and say it's no big deal, really.
games.why: Harjit's rule: answer the question that was actually asked, kindly, in one breath. faith at work isn't a speech.

practice: Find something you wear or carry every day: a ring, a watch, a hair tie, a kara. Hold it and notice its weight, its temperature, the small sound it makes if you tap it. Then put it back on and sit with it there.

wordCard.voice: Faith at the workplace. Keeping your articles of faith on at work, and explaining them kindly when someone asks.

carryVoice: Keep this one: faith at work, kept on and explained in one kind breath. See you tomorrow.
